title: Rama's naming day
hookLine: Vasishtha names four baby princes; why Hindu families mark a name, a first bite and a first haircut
last: SATTVIC FOOD: SIMPLE, AND GIVEN WITH LOVE.

cards: Ayodhya. For years King Dasharatha has had no children. Then, after a great fire offering, his three queens give birth to four sons, and the whole city pours into the streets to celebrate.
On the eleventh day, the family's sage, Vasishtha, sits with the babies to name them. The eldest: Rama, the one who brings delight. Then Bharata.
Then the twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna, the slayer of enemies. A whole kingdom stops to name four babies.

teach.b: That's the Ramayana, and Vasishtha doesn't stop at names: the epic says he performed all the princes' childhood rites. Those rites are samskaras, and they're the teaching today.
The word means a finishing, a polishing, the way raw metal is worked until it shines. In Hindu life, samskaras mark the steps of a person's life, from before birth to after death.
Later lists often count sixteen, though the lists differ, and most families keep only some. You may have been through a few without knowing their names.
Namakarana, the naming, often on the eleventh or twelfth day, like Rama's. Annaprashana, the first bite of solid food, usually rice, at around six months.

teach.h: A FIRST BITE, A FIRST HAIRCUT.
teach.b: Chudakarana, the first haircut, which many families call mundan, in the first or third year by family custom. A toddler wails, the barber is quick, and a grandmother catches every curl.
The birth hair is shaved away, a fresh start, and many families offer it at a temple or a holy river.
Vidyarambha, the start of learning: a child traces first letters, often in a plate of rice, on a day for Saraswati, the goddess of learning.
It's why so many kids were taught to touch a book they've stepped on, then their forehead. And the wedding gets its own day soon. Here's what they share.

Each takes an ordinary first and says: God is part of this. The child is being polished, step by step, the way a kingdom stopped for Rama. So the next time a family chat pings about a mundan, it isn't just a haircut.

how: Many Hindu families keep some of the samskaras: a naming ceremony, the first feeding of rice (annaprashana), the first haircut (mundan or chudakarana), often at a temple, and a first-letters ceremony honoring Saraswati.

games.q: which rite is which — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're at your nephew's mundan. he's wailing, the barber is fast, and grandma is catching the hair in a cloth. what happens to the hair in many families?
o: it goes out with the trash.
it's offered at a temple or a holy river.
games.why: many families offer the first hair at a temple or a sacred river: a fresh start, given away.

practice: Remember a first that someone marked for you: a first day of school, a first bike ride, a birthday, a photo someone kept, and picture who was there and who made the fuss.
You may only remember the story told about it, and that's fine; breathe in the fact that someone thought your small step was worth stopping for. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Samskara. A polishing: the rites that make the steps of a life holy, from a name to a first bite of rice to a first haircut. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a finishing, a polishing; the rites that mark the steps of a life.

carryVoice: Your line: samskaras make life's steps holy. A kingdom stopped to name Rama. Day one hundred twenty-nine, marked.
